extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and policymakers considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution; readers interested in constitutional design and federal-state relations
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of federal powers and state restrictions
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and justification of certain federal powers and restrictions on State authority in the proposed U.S. Constitution, with practical examples and rhetorical defense aimed at persuading citizens to ratify. Covers naturalization, bankruptcy, interstate recognition of records, intellectual property, federal district jurisdiction, treason, admission of new states, guarantees/protections, assumption of debts, amendment/ratification rules, and prohibitions on State actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish a uniform rule of naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizes the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevents inconsistent State naturalization rules that would allow persons qualified as citizens in one State to evade incapacities in another, avoids conflict where residence in one State confers rights in another, and remedies defects of the Confederation that produced delicate and intricate questions. The power is presented as a necessary correction to varied State practices that could create serious embarrassments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizes Congress to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: closely connected with regulation of commerce and prevents many frauds where parties or property may be moved across State lines; the expediency is presented as clear and unlikely to be questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prescribe proof and interstate effect of public acts, records, and judicial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may by general laws prescribe the manner in which public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and their effect in other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: an improvement on the indeterminate Confederation clause; can be a convenient instrument of justice, particularly beneficial on borders of contiguous States to prevent sudden, secret translation of effects during process. Emphasizes clarity and inter-jurisdictional cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish post roads
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may establish post roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: characterized as harmless and likely productive of great public convenience; facilitates intercourse between the States and is deemed worthy of public care if judiciously managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to promote progress of science and useful arts (copyrights and patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may 'promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: utility scarcely questioned; copyrights have been recognized in common law, and inventions reasonably belong to inventors. The public good coincides with individual claims. States cannot separately make effectual provisions; most States already made such laws at Congress' instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive federal legislation over federal district and federal properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to exercise exclusive legislation ... over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) ... the seat of the government' and 'over all places purchased ... for erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: indispensable necessity of complete authority at the seat of government to prevent insult/interruption of public authority and dependency of federal officers on state protection. Consent of ceding State and protections for inhabitants (compacts, municipal legislature, voice in elections) are emphasized to obviate objections. Similar need for federal control over military/security sites to protect public property and national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to declare punishment of treason with limits on attainder and corruption of blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attainted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: federal authority to punish treason is necessary; limitation on attainder and corruption of blood guards against 'new-fangled and artificial treasons' used by violent factions. The constitutional definition and proof requirements are portrayed as barriers to abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to admit new States with restrictions on formation without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may 'admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent' of the legislatures concerned and of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: fills omission in the Articles of Confederation; the concurrence requirement is consonant with principles of fairness and quiets jealousies of larger and smaller States by preventing partition or forced junctions without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to dispose of and regulate federal territory and property
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may 'dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States,' with proviso that nothing shall prejudice claims of the U.S. or any State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: important power required for similar considerations as federal district authority; proviso addresses jealousies and outstanding questions concerning Western territory; presented as necessary for management and to avoid prejudice to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee of a republican form of government to each State
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government must 'guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a confederacy founded on republican principles should have a superintending government able to defend the system against aristocratic/monarchical innovations. The guarantee presupposes an existing republican form; it does not permit federal alteration beyond ensuring states remain 'republican' rather than 'antirepublican.' The provision aims to preserve compatible forms across the union while allowing States to change to other republican forms if they choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal protection against invasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal obligation 'to protect each of them [the States] against invasion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: society owes protection to its parts; language secures each State against foreign hostility and ambitious enterprises by more powerful neighbors. Historical examples show weaker members benefit from such guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal aid against domestic violence on application
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal protection 'on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: mutual aid against insurrections and domestic disorders is appropriate; federal interposition is limited, bound to pursue its guaranty and to support States where local authority cannot suppress violence. Addresses concerns that this could justify improper alteration of State governments—explains the federal role is remedial, not a license for unwarranted change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of pre-Constitution debts and engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress shall 'consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: declaratory clause intended to assure foreign creditors and reflect that engagements are reciprocal; defense against fears the new government could repudiate obligations. Emphasized as a reassurance rather than a novel grant of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for amendments ratified by three fourths of the States with limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: balances adaptability with stability—guards against both extreme facility and extreme difficulty in altering the Constitution. The two exceptions (one mentioned as protecting equality of suffrage in the Senate) protect residual State sovereignty; amendment power can be originated by general or State governments. Presented as a prudent mechanism for future correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification by nine State conventions sufficient to establish Constitution among ratifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States ratifying the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: requiring unanimity would give undue veto power to one member; necessity and self-preservation justify non-unanimous adoption. Addresses delicate questions of whether the Confederation can be superseded without unanimous consent (answered by necessity, principles of compact and treaty law) and the relation between ratifying and non-ratifying States (no political relation but moral obligations and hopes for moderation and reunion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States entering into treaties, alliances, or confederations
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: copied from existing Articles of Union; prevents States from interfering with uniform foreign policy and protects national responsibility. Presented as an obvious and necessary restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States granting letters of marque and reprisal (except by U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'grant letters of marque and reprisal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: extends former rule (which permitted States to grant letters of marque after declaration of war) to require central licensing both during peace and war; justified by need for uniformity in foreign affairs and national accountability for conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States coining money
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'coin money.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: leaving coinage to States would multiply expensive mints and diversify forms and weights of circulating pieces, impeding intercourse among States; central control prevents conflicting currencies and preserves stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States emitting bills of credit (issuing paper money)
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'emit bills of credit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: paper money has had 'pestilent effects' on confidence between people and in public councils, on industry, morals, and republican government; prohibition responds to recent harmful State practices and prevents similar abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States making anything but gold and silver legal tender
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: same principle as removing coinage and issuing paper money—prevents retrospective alterations in value and consequent injury to citizens of other States and foreign subjects; preserves uniformity and prevents animosities among States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing obligations of contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: these measures are contrary to first principles of the social compact and sound legislation; additional constitutional fences guard personal security and private rights and protect against legislative speculations and repeated interferences that would undermine industry and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States granting titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall 'grant any title of nobility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: copied from the Articles of Confederation; needs no further comment—meant to prevent aristocratic distinctions within republican polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States laying imposts or duties on imports or exports without Congress' consent (with limited exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws; net produce of such duties shall be for use of the U.S. Treasury; such laws subject to revision and control of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: restraint enforces the need for federal regulation of trade; qualification allows reasonable discretion for States' inspection needs while ensuring a federal check against abuse; revenues directed to the national treasury and laws subject to federal revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States laying duties on tonnage without Congress' consent
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: part of the package of restraints necessary to submit regulation of trade and navigation to federal councils and to maintain uniformity and national control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States keeping troops or ships of war in time of peace without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevents individual States from maintaining independent military establishments in peacetime which could threaten the union or other States; part of ensuring national security and uniform military policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States entering agreements or compacts with other States or foreign powers without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevents States from undermining national foreign policy or entering into compacts that conflict with federal interests; consistent with necessity of central coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States engaging in war except under limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall ... engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prevents unilateral State war-making except in immediate self-defense, preserving national coherence in foreign relations and reducing risk of inter-State or foreign entanglements arising from individual State actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper Clause (power to make all laws necessary and proper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and defense: without this power the Constitution would be a 'dead letter.' Explains and rejects alternative formulations (express-only, exhaustive positive enumeration, negative enumeration, or silence) as impracticable. Argues that the means necessary to effect general ends must be authorized; acknowledges potential for misconstruction but points to checks: executive and judiciary interpretation, state vigilance, and ultimate redress via the people through elections. Emphasizes that the clause is indispensable for functional government.
